sources.headline: Today’s irreverent politics ignore ancient wisdom: The need to know your limits
sources.text:
A common complaint today laments the “shamelessness” of politicians. Until recently, the argument goes, more elected officials had a sense of shame to hold them back from ugly words and deeds, at least in public. Many in the current crop, however, seem to have no fear of disgrace; they revel in contempt for the niceties of old – unwritten rules against cursing, slander or lying, but also written rules against abuse of power.
The problem isn’t so much a question of bad manners or even of corruption. It’s really about leadership.
I study the history of political thought and work on the psychology of lawfulness: the character traits citizens need for the rule of law to work. One such trait is each person’s ability to limit herself – to revere some larger principle that she would be ashamed to betray.
That’s all the more true for good leaders, even in a constitutional republic defined by checks and balances. Sometimes decisions need to be made over the objections of partisan opposition or of another branch of government. But the public can trust decision-makers only if those leaders check themselves.
Like many problems, political shamelessness may seem new, but thinkers stretching back to the ancient Greeks have warned of its perils, which they described as “irreverence” – the failure to respect something bigger than ourselves. If today’s politics seem threatened by some such menace, it may be because we are neglecting this ancient wisdom.
Awaken to our ignorance
Perhaps the most searching account of this problem and what to do about it can be found in a work by the Greek philosopher Plato, who died in 347 B.C.E. The text is known simply as the “Laws.”
Like his better-known “Republic,” the “Laws” envisions a “city in speech”: a utopia, a place that exists only in theory. But whereas the city of the “Republic” is ruled autocratically by “philosopher kings,” the “Laws” explores the possibilities and limitations of what is now called constitutional government.
Plato’s ‘Laws,’ written almost 2,400 years ago, explores what is now called constitutional government.
Codex Parisinus graecus 1807/Bibliothèque Nationale via Wikimedia Commons
All of Plato’s writings suggest that the most significant political fact is the scarcity of wisdom: the dearth of knowledge needed to live a flourishing human life. What’s more, he taught, most of us don’t recognize our own ignorance – indeed, we powerfully resist recognizing it.
Plato’s “Laws” examines the rule of law in light of this fact. It teaches that the function of law is to awaken citizens and politicians to their own ignorance and then to point them to a wise, ethical authority.
At its best, law wouldn’t just protect security or individual rights. It would provoke people to recognize their profound need of a standard of good and bad beyond their own judgment.
Otherwise, human nature being what it is, Plato saw that each person would corruptly “honor his own” – himself and everything connected to him – “more than the truth.” He would rationalize his own prejudices and justify his own selfishness.
Reverence as a virtue
In the “Laws,” the antidote to this problem is what Plato calls “aidos,” or reverence: the virtue governing shame, as well as awe. Taken by themselves, shame and awe are neither laudable nor blameworthy. But to have reverence, Plato suggests, is to feel these emotions for the right reasons.
Shame and awe go together for Plato because they both involve a feeling of diminishment: a sense of our own limits. With shame, this feeling is social, connected to the fear of someone else’s disapproving gaze. With awe, the feeling of smallness is inspired by something that makes our own concerns and capacities seem trivial – something like God or the divine.
Feeling small – in a good way.
wilpunt/E+ via Getty Images
It might seem as though a virtuous person would not feel shame; she would simply never do or say anything shameful. But in Plato’s eyes, precious few achieve so pure a virtue. For most, fear of shame is a necessary backstop to push people away from what wrongly tempts them. Likewise, awe prevents people from underestimating difficult tasks or from overestimating themselves.
According to the “Laws,” the proper object of reverence is wisdom, represented as God: “the measure of all things.” The text stresses the awesome nature of the wisdom needed to judge things well – the need to look for truth outside ourselves. It teaches that we should be ashamed to “measure” things by reference only to our own fallible judgment.
Awesome responsibility
Reverence might seem irrelevant to modern politics. In liberal democracies, public life is devoted to securing liberty, not to learning virtue. Shaming people for disregarding the awesome nature of wisdom might appear a gross violation of their freedom of conscience. Modern societies can scarcely agree on what is shameful to begin with.
Reverence might also seem to involve a piety that is out of place in a diverse democracy. Many people believe in God, but political decisions are judged by secular standards like their popularity, or by whether they benefit the public interest.
Nevertheless, I would argue that modern politics continue to depend on something akin to reverence. Liberal democracies might not use government to teach virtue directly, but they do need citizens and statesmen who appreciate the limits of their own judgment and their need of higher principles to guide their decisions.
It helps that awe need not be inspired by gods – or wisdom, which was what Plato truly revered. Citizens might feel awe, for example, at the enormous responsibility of self-government. As philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau wrote in the 18th century, democracy is more suited to gods than men: rightly understood, it is demanding in the highest degree.
People vote in the primary election at Northwestern High School in Detroit on Aug. 4, 2026.
AP Photo/Nic Antaya
Modern liberty is especially demanding; it isn’t only a matter of having a right to vote or speak our minds, as important as such rights may be. It is also a matter of having to choose between myriad ethical, religious and cultural traditions, or to choose none at all.
Such freedom is both a boon and a burden. In today’s democracies, citizens are responsible for their own ethical lives: for determining what should count as right and wrong, good and bad.
But it is precisely because we are free to waste our freedom, Plato might say, that we need reverence all the more: feeling awe for the responsibility of using that freedom well, and shame when we do not. As for political leaders, until they cease to find an approving audience for their contempt of principled behavior, the shamelessness that many observers find so disturbing will likely continue.

sources.headline: Now We’re Seeing the Extent of American Decay
sources.text:
In an age of unrelenting and seemingly accelerating demands on one’s attention, knowing what to reserve outrage for is becoming one of life’s most difficult challenges. Never has this been more apparent than in the wake of the last week or so’s political news from the United States.
The latest onslaught began with the spectacle of U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who strutted about last Thursday as he announced his plans to livestream the execution by firing squad of a former U.S. military officer convicted by court-martial and sentenced to death for the terrorist murder of 12 fellow soldiers and a civilian at Fort Hood in 2009.
In an age of unrelenting and seemingly accelerating demands on one’s attention, knowing what to reserve outrage for is becoming one of life’s most difficult challenges. Never has this been more apparent than in the wake of the last week or so’s political news from the United States.
The latest onslaught began with the spectacle of U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who strutted about last Thursday as he announced his plans to livestream the execution by firing squad of a former U.S. military officer convicted by court-martial and sentenced to death for the terrorist murder of 12 fellow soldiers and a civilian at Fort Hood in 2009.
It is not clear whether Hegseth, a man who seems to take crudeness as a virtue, researched the history of state executions before going public with this plan. If he had, he would have quickly learned two things that would give a sensible and morally informed defense secretary pause: The U.S. military hasn’t performed a public execution in 90 years, and the countries that continue to enact rituals like these, such as Iran and Afghanistan under the Taliban, head the list of nations that the United States has long routinely deplored as barbaric. Credit Hegseth for understanding his boss, though. Asked if he supported public executions, U.S. President Donald Trump replied with a single word: “Absolutely.”
A day after Hegseth’s announcement, following the Norwegian Nobel Committee’s decision to select the former United Nations high commissioner for human rights, Navi Pillay, as its latest peace laureate, the Trump administration slammed Norway for the choice and announced that it would take punitive actions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), where Pillay had once served as a judge. Trump complained that Pillay had been plucked from obscurity and said that he was the person who deserved the prize most for having ended eight wars around the world.
Here, the outrages compound themselves. Norway may be where the committee is based, but it does not decide the prize winners. Pillay is far from unknown, especially for anyone who values international human rights. And Trump’s peacemaking claims are as dubious as any of the lies and distortions of fact that routinely pepper his public comments.
Beyond the U.S. president’s bottomless neediness and thirst for recognition, Washington’s outrage against Pillay seems largely based on her leadership of a U.N. commission that reviewed Israel’s post-Oct. 7, 2023, offensive in Gaza, concluding that the killing of tens of thousands of Palestinians and the wholesale devastation of the territory’s housing and infrastructure had constituted a genocide. One can only read between the lines in trying to discern the true motivations behind the timing of the newly announced U.S. sanctions against the ICC, but it appears to be retaliation for Pillay sharing information from the U.N. commission with the ICC, which has issued arrest warrants for Israeli politicians, including Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. This was certainly Netanyahu’s sense of things, for he promptly congratulated the Trump administration for its actions against the ICC.
For a long time now, in the aftermath of Hamas’s barbaric and murderous attack that killed roughly 1,200 Israelis and took approximately 250 hostage three years ago, both the Biden and Trump administrations have failed their ally Israel by neither forcefully condemning nor effectively restraining its military actions in Gaza that were hugely disproportionate and grossly indiscriminate.
One can debate the label genocide, but to single out the ICC and Pillay is both self-defeating and immoral. A wide array of groups and experts, many of them Jewish and some Israeli, have reached similar conclusions about a genocide in Gaza. The United States has never articulated a coherent, substantive response to this, seeming to think that it is sufficient to say that Israel is its ally and friend. This amounts to an abandonment of U.S. values—something the country once staked its international standing on, even if it frequently fell short of its own high-sounding ideals.
Beyond conflicting views about Israel and Palestine, though, the United States attack on the ICC, like its hostility toward the U.N. and its rapidly eroding commitment to other global institutions and norms, is pushing the world in a dangerous direction, where rules matter less and less and naked might is given precedence over considerations of what is principled, or right.
Further evidence of this shift, not drift, can also be seen in Trump’s extraordinarily crude transactional moves toward Russia and Ukraine in recent days. Worried that persistently high diesel and gasoline prices in the United States will imperil his party’s chances in the upcoming midterm elections, Trump suspended sanctions on Moscow to hastily arrange a fuel delivery deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin. This will boost Russian revenues at a time when its war of aggression in Ukraine has begun crippling its economy.
Trump also denounced Ukraine, the victim in this conflict, for defending itself by attacking Russia’s petroleum infrastructure. It didn’t matter to him that these were reprisals for Russia’s savage and much more systematic attacks on Ukraine’s energy systems and economy. Trump, who has long displayed a poorly explained attraction to Putin, responded to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s complaints about the Trump-Putin deal by saying it was time for Ukraine to replace its leader, a long-standing Russian demand.
The most recent outrage is geopolitically minor but speaks just as powerfully to the moral rot in Washington. That is the scandal surrounding the newly resigned U.S. ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle. Even the Trump administration couldn’t overlook the discrediting appearance of an envoy who has been accused of soliciting payment from a political fundraiser in exchange for facilitating high-level access to the U.S. government. Guilfoyle claims her innocence. The evidence against her, as first reported in the Wall Street Journal, includes text messages that seem to clearly point to a pay-to-play deal.
If she committed the acts she is accused of, Guilfoyle is hardly alone in her greed and audacity. As I have written before, corruption is the defining characteristic of this administration, one in which diplomatic envoys such as Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff pursue private business deals in the very countries where they are negotiating. Not to mention that one of Trump’s sons recently accepted a gift from a shadowy Russian oligarch to finance his lavish post-wedding party in the Caribbean. The man, said to be close to Putin, scarcely speaks English, yet Donald Trump Jr.’s representatives initially described him as a close friend.
If, taken together, things like these seem to bespeak U.S. decline, there is yet one more incident that does so even more loudly: the pervasive self-congratulation and denial emanating from today’s Washington. This could be heard clearly in the mishmash of a speech that Trump’s secretary of state, Marco Rubio, gave in Athens last week. In it, he strung together a middle school student’s gloss of the greatest hits of Western civilization, as he claimed the United States to be a direct descendant of ancient Greece and a paragon of Western ideals that span from that civilization’s early democracy to the Enlightenment.
Rubio’s worst pretension, though, was to speak to Europe as if the United States under Trump serves as an inspiring model for that continent. “We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was lit here millennia ago,” Rubio said, standing with the Parthenon glowing in the background.
Europeans may still share a proverbial bed with the United States, but it is hard to imagine that their dreams could be more different. Instead, many are hoping that a United States that increasingly appears lost and valueless can rediscover what they have admired in it throughout much of its history before it is too late.

Democracy Is Not Silence Between Elections

A vote gives a government the authority to rule. It does not give it the right to silence the people.

By Nabeel Kolothumthodi
October 14, 2026
 
 
 
 

Screenshot of a video of Delhi Police beating protesters with batons in New Delhi, India, June 20, 2026.

Credit: X/Rahul Gandhi
Ad
Subscribe for ads-free reading

In a democracy, an election’s credibility depends not only on the votes cast by citizens, but also on their confidence in the institution responsible for conducting it. India’s Election Commission (EC), a constitutional body entrusted with safeguarding the integrity of elections, is therefore expected to stand above partisan interests. Yet, allegations by opposition parties and activists that the EC has favored the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in elections as well as processes determining who can vote, alongside questions about electoral transparency and institutional independence, have brought this constitutional responsibility into sharp public debate.

The concern extends beyond any single election or political party. When citizens begin to question whether institutions designed to act independently are functioning impartially, the issue becomes larger than electoral competition. There is something deeply political about being made to stand outside, whether outside parliament, outside a university auditorium, outside government offices, or outside the very institutions that claim to represent you. In a democracy, the distinction between being inside and outside is never merely geographical.

India is a constitutional republic founded on popular sovereignty. The opening words of its Constitution, “We, the People of India,” establish that political authority ultimately derives from the people. Yet, we often reduce democracy to a single moment, the casting of a vote. We elect our representatives, celebrate electoral victories and expect the machinery of governance to function. But what happens between elections? What happens when citizens believe their representatives have failed them? What happens when people must stand outside the corridors of power to make themselves heard? A vote determines who governs. But a voice determines whether those who govern remain accountable.

Disagreement is natural in a plural society. The problem arises when criticism is treated as disloyalty, opposition to government policy is confused with opposition to the nation, and peaceful protest is viewed as a threat simply because it challenges authority. A government may win an election, but it cannot claim ownership of the republic.

When the People Challenge Power

India’s democratic history cannot be told through elections and parliamentary proceedings alone. It must also be told through the people who marched, organized, protested, and challenged the established order. The freedom struggle transformed streets, villages, and public spaces into arenas of resistance against colonial rule. Ordinary people did not wait for permission from those in power to demand freedom. Their participation was central to the making of independent India.

One of the most consequential examples of public resistance in contemporary India was the anti-corruption movement led by Anna Hazare and his colleagues in 2011. During Prime Minister Manmohan Singh’s tenure, thousands gathered at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar and then at Ramlila Maidan demanding a strong Lokpal institution to investigate corruption. The movement emerged amid major corruption controversies and growing public dissatisfaction with the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance government.

The confrontation was not without controversy. Hazare was arrested in August 2011 during a hunger strike, provoking further demonstrations. Yet, the movement could not simply be dismissed. Public pressure brought institutional accountability to the center of national debate, and the UPA government enacted the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act in 2013. The movement also contributed to the wider anti-establishment sentiment preceding the 2014 change of government, although it was not the sole cause of that electoral outcome.

Ad

The Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (MKSS) movement stands as another powerful reminder that democracy is not secured by elections alone, but by citizens’ ability to question power. Beginning in Rajasthan, rural workers and farmers peacefully demanded access to official records on wages and development spending, exposing corruption through jan sunwais (public hearings) and a historic 40-day dharna (sit-in) at Beawar in Rajasthan in 1996. Their discipline, courage and refusal to retreat showed that a protest can transform a local grievance into a national democratic demand.

The first UPA government responded by enacting the Right to Information Act in 2005, converting a citizen’s moral claim into a legal right. This landmark law empowered ordinary Indians to inspect government records and hold public authorities accountable, proving that protest remains essential to protecting transparency, justice, and democracy itself.

The lesson is significant. A government can disagree with a movement, but it cannot expect public anger to disappear merely by containing it. The MKSS movement demonstrated how resistance can compel political institutions to confront uncomfortable questions. Democracy is strengthened when public demands find meaningful institutional responses.

The same lesson emerges from the defense of civil liberties during the Emergency of 1975-77. The suspension of fundamental freedoms and restrictions on the media demonstrated how quickly democratic institutions can be weakened when political authority becomes concentrated.

The electoral defeat of Indira Gandhi’s government in 1977 subsequently showed that citizens could use the ballot to reject authoritarian excesses. Indian democracy has endured not because dissent disappeared, but because people continued to demand their constitutional rights.

Dissent Is Not Disloyalty

The Constitution guarantees freedom of speech and expression and the right to assemble peacefully and without arms under Article 19, subject to constitutionally permitted reasonable restrictions. These freedoms are not absolute, but restrictions cannot become a convenient instrument for silencing criticism. In Amit Sahni v. Commissioner of Police (2020), concerning the Shaheen Bagh protest in the national capital, New Delhi, the Supreme Court addressed the limits of indefinitely occupying public ways. The democratic challenge is to protect peaceful dissent while respecting the rights of other citizens.

Recent events in India’s neighborhood offer a sobering warning. In Bangladesh in 2024, student protests over government job quotas escalated into a wider uprising against Sheikh Hasina’s government. A violent crackdown and mounting public anger preceded her resignation and departure from the country. Likewise, Nepal’s Gen Z-led protests in 2025 exposed the dangers of political alienation and declining public confidence in established leadership.

These events are not templates for India, nor should violence be romanticized. India’s political and societal culture is different. They demonstrate, however, that suppressing grievances does not necessarily extinguish them. When peaceful channels of dissent are obstructed, institutions fail to respond, and citizens lose faith in the possibility of change, a political crisis can grow beyond the control of those governing. Governments that mistake silence for consent may discover too late that public anger has merely accumulated.

Democracy is not merely an administrative arrangement; it is an inheritance secured through struggle and sacrifice. A republic needs institutions where decisions are made, but it also needs doors that remain open, and institutions willing to listen when concerns go unanswered. A vote is an act of citizenship, but so is a question put to a minister, an investigation published by an independent journalist, a student assembly, a worker’s march, or a peaceful protest outside the gates of power.

The republic belongs as much to the critic as to the supporter, and as much to the citizen standing outside as to the representative seated inside. Its strength will be measured not only by how people vote, but by whether they remain free to speak afterwards, and whether those in power are willing to listen. A vote gives a government the authority to rule. It does not give it the right to silence the people.

sources.headline: Obama says drift towards extremism 'not inevitable'
sources.text: Obama said that during his presidential campaign in 2008, when social media and technology was gaining traction, he had seen them as a beacon for hopeBut he said the same positive forces and tools that could mobilise people around democracy or human rights could also be used by hate groups.He said they "connected people for good, but also for ill"."It turns out that the reptilian side of our brain really gets attracted to anger, fear, resentment and the sense that someone is out to get you," he said."So a lot of social media and a lot of our information is informed around that."But the former president, who has already spoken in Belfast and will appear in Manchester on Thursday night, said that a drift towards extremism was "not inevitable".He added: "After World War Two, at least in the United States and certainly in Europe as well, the federal government said 'we're going to set up some rules because we've seen what propaganda can do in the hands of somebody like Hitler. "We can see how big lies and misinformation can distort and enrage and incite violence. So we're going to hold these folks responsible'.""We have not chosen to do that."Speaking about hope, Obama was asked if he still believed in a Martin Luther King Jr phrase he quoted years ago, about the arm of the moral universe being long, but ultimately bending towards justice.The former president said that he still stands by the quote and argued that hope is an active "almost theological" choice people must make.He said: "It is a decision about how do we face and embrace this finite amount of time we have on the planet." He told the audience he believes it is healthier for people to believe that change is possible."I think when we act on that basis, it doesn't always work out, but over time things do get better," he said.Obama also said there seems to be a cycle in humanity where people forget lessons learned from the past and start to take things for granted."We start thinking 'maybe using language in public from our politicians that fosters hatred and scapegoats certain people – immigrants, Jews, or blacks or gays – that's just talk, it's humour'."He said people forget where that can lead to, with them becoming less tolerant.Obama told the audience that the world is going to be dealing with "big challenges", but he said he thinks "we can be better" and that making the world better remains worth fighting for.

sources.headline: After Iran, Washington Needs a New Basing Strategy
sources.text:
For a generation, the United States has relied on large military bases across the Persian Gulf to project power, confident that they were beyond the reach of groups such as the Islamic State and that Iran, despite its growing missile arsenal, would not risk a sustained attack on them. The Iran war has shattered that assumption, with Iranian missiles and drones repeatedly striking those bases and forcing the U.S. military to empty facilities it has operated for decades.
Now the Pentagon is weighing whether to rebuild and harden those bases or shift its force presence westward, including to Jordan and Israel, farther from Iran’s reach. It should do neither. Both approaches assume that projecting power in the Middle East requires large, permanent bases, even as the war has shown otherwise.
The United States waged one of its largest air campaigns in decades, flying more than 10,200 sorties and conducting more than 13,500 strikes, in the first 38 days of Operation Epic Fury, despite Iran’s repeated strikes on key sites. The campaign never paused, however, because U.S. forces quickly shifted operations elsewhere when bases came under attack.
For instance, anticipating an attack on Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, the largest U.S. military facility in the Middle East, the United States pulled its personnel and ran the air war from Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina instead. When Iran struck Al Udeid’s Combined Air Operations Center, which had run U.S. air campaigns in the region since 2003, it was already empty. Equipment moved, too. In the days before the war, the Air Force began sending aerial refueling tankers to Ben Gurion, Israel’s main civilian airport, where they operated using existing airfield infrastructure, supported by specialized maintenance personnel and equipment brought in as needed.
That ability to keep fighting even as forward bases were evacuated or damaged may be the war’s most important lesson for U.S. force posture in the Middle East. What mattered was not large, permanent bases but access to a range of airfields, including civilian ones, and the capacity to move aircraft, personnel, equipment, and munitions among them when bases came under attack. Instead of pouring billions of dollars into repairing bases or building new ones farther west, Washington should use this opportunity to rethink its approach, trading its permanent sites for a lighter, more modular posture that better aligns with the future of warfare in the Middle East and beyond.
Neither rebuilding Gulf bases nor moving them west would fix the fundamental problems, which have been painfully exposed in recent months: These bases are easy for an adversary to find, expensive to defend, and not always available when Washington needs them.
Simply put, there is no hiding a permanent base. An adversary has years to study its layout, and Iran has used that time to determine where and when to strike. For instance, on March 27, Iran destroyed an E-3 Sentry, one of the few command-and-control planes in the U.S. Air Force’s inventory, at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia. Iran has also targeted operations centers, hangars, barracks, and fuel depots across multiple U.S. bases, suggesting detailed knowledge of their layouts and operations.
Defending these fixed positions against missile and drone attacks has come at a high, asymmetric price. In the war’s first six weeks, the United States burned through more than 1,000 interceptors, including more than 40 percent of its prewar Patriot stocks and about half of its THAADs.
Hardening bases would not solve the problem, nor would it come cheap. Reinforced shelters and buried fuel tanks can protect some assets, but tankers and early-warning aircraft are too large for anything but the largest and most expensive shelters. Whether Washington spends billions of dollars hardening bases or burns through costly interceptors defending them, it will be paying far more than Iran does to attack them.
Shifting bases west to Jordan and Israel would merely relocate the problem, as both are still within range of Iranian missiles. Additional permanent U.S. facilities in either country would give Tehran another set of targets to map and more reason to expand its medium-range missile and long-range drone stocks.
A westward shift would also come with added political risks. Israel in particular has repeatedly engaged in risky military behavior that puts it at odds with Washington. In August, it bombed an air base in northern Syria near the Turkish border without warning the United States—an attack the U.S. ambassador to Turkey called an “unnecessary escalation” and suggested could be meant to bait Turkey, a NATO ally, into a wider war. The United States already incurs entanglement costs from its alliance with Israel, but a large, permanent basing presence would compound them, exposing U.S. forces to retaliation for Israeli actions, potentially pulling the United States into Israel’s next war, and further straining relations with Arab partners.
Nor do permanent bases guarantee that a host country will let the United States use them when it needs them most. In May, as the United States began an operation to escort commercial ships through the Strait of Hormuz, relying heavily on aircraft flying from Gulf countries, Saudi Arabia and Kuwait temporarily restricted U.S. access. Saudi officials were reportedly alarmed that Washington was downplaying Iranian attacks on Gulf states and doubted the United States would protect them if the fighting escalated. Not long after, in July, Israel capped the number of U.S. tankers at Ben Gurion to avoid crowding out summer tourist traffic, forcing the Air Force to move jets elsewhere.
Both episodes show how quickly the United States can lose access when a host decides its interests lie elsewhere, even where Washington has long-standing bases or close strategic ties.
Washington has a rare opportunity to reevaluate its basing strategy, and instead of doubling down on permanent bases, it should work to secure access to a wide variety of airports and host-country air bases across the Gulf, in Europe, and around the edges of the Middle East. Some of these airfields would be major hubs, with the ramp space, fuel, and cargo-handling equipment to support large logistical movements. Others might offer little more than a lit runway, parking space for aircraft, fuel, and a place to store munitions, with U.S. personnel deployed only in a crisis. This is a more resilient posture because no single host government’s refusal would be enough to ground U.S. air operations and Iran would have far more locations to track and target.
Think of access as buying options on the stock market: For a relatively small premium, Washington can preserve choices for a crisis without paying the political, economic, and military costs of maintaining forces at every deployed location in peacetime. Keeping most forces at home would also leave them better prepared, with deeper technical and personal support that deployed units must do without. While forces train and gain readiness at home, much of what they need for contingencies could be stationed forward in the region. The United States could preposition weapons, equipment, and fuel at select sites; keep other supplies afloat; and rehearse surging forces into the region, dispersing them among multiple locations and shifting them when threatened.
That hedge is as much political as technological. Today, against adversaries with limited surveillance and long-range strike capacity, dispersal has a significant advantage because it complicates targeting. As surveillance improves and long-range arsenals grow, that advantage will diminish. In a world of ubiquitous sensors, there will be fewer places to hide, and the balance could eventually swing back to a few heavily fortified strongholds. That uncertainty is reason enough to hesitate before committing resources to a single posture.
This approach could also strengthen deterrence. If Iran has learned anything from this war, it is that large U.S. bases are likely to be emptied once fighting begins. That knowledge weakens the deterrent signals those bases once sent and, in turn, undercuts the strategic case for maintaining them. Deterrence requires Washington to credibly demonstrate that it can bring enough military power to bear to deny Iran its political and military objectives, but that does not mean keeping tens of thousands of U.S. forces permanently forward.
Still, a lighter posture designed to surge is not without trade-offs. Forces based outside the region would take longer to arrive and would increase demands on strategic airlift, aerial refueling, and other logistics at the start of a crisis. Keeping a wide network of airfields ready would also require continuous attention, from maintaining agreements with hosts to managing prepositioned stocks.
But the posture would come with readiness gains as well. Units rotating in for regular exercises would train more often with partner militaries and practice the same kinds of operations U.S. forces expect to rely on in the Indo-Pacific, flowing reinforcements into the theater in a crisis and then operating from dispersed locations under threat. Ultimately, whatever speed is lost matters less in the Middle East than it would elsewhere.
Tehran is not trying to rapidly seize and hold territory, making the current war a different military problem from the one Washington faces in Europe or the Pacific, where the fear is that Russia or China could present the United States with a territorial fait accompli. Instead, Tehran wields missiles, drones, proxies, and threats to Gulf shipping to pressure its neighbors into making political concessions. Coercion of this kind takes time to work, meaning Washington can respond from farther away, whether by sending forces into the region, supporting partners, or striking, without exposing U.S. troops to unnecessary risks within range of Iran’s missiles.
Offshore balancing is not a new idea. What is new is the wartime evidence that it can work. U.S. bases in the Middle East once served a deterrent purpose, but they are now less a symbol of strength than a collection of fixed targets Iran knows how to attack. Now is a good time for Washington to ask whether continuing its current posture still serves U.S. interests or is simply inertia.

sources.headline: Do the Benefits Outweigh the Risks of Hosting U.S. Military Bases?
sources.text:
Since the end of World War II, the United States has maintained hundreds of military installations abroad. While U.S. forces have faced some objections to their presence, many allies and partners have seen U.S. bases and other facilities on their territory as a sign of their close relations with a superpower, a form of protection, and an economic boon. However, the war with Iran has raised questions about whether hosting U.S. military installations subjects Arab Gulf states to Iranian retaliation while failing to provide sufficient protection. The sudden withdrawal of U.S. B-1 bombers from the RAF Fairford site in the United Kingdom earlier this month — reportedly in response to an Iranian threat — highlighted the risks to host countries. The Trump administration’s approach to allies and partners — such as criticizing European countries, scaling back military exercises with South Korea, and calling on Arab Gulf states to pay the United States for its help protecting ships transiting through the Strait of Hormuz — has not helped to reinforce public support for hosting U.S. military sites.We asked five experts about how some crucial U.S. allies and partners view hosting U.S. forces today, particularly in the wake of the war with Iran. Is the shine wearing off, or do the benefits still outweigh the disadvantages?For their assessments of the view from Japan, South Korea, Qatar, Germany, and the United Kingdom, read more below.Ayumi Teraoka Assistant Professor of Politics at Brandeis University Nonresident Senior Fellow at the Foreign Policy Research InstituteThe war in Iran highlights two concerns for Tokyo about U.S. reliability: inadequate U.S. consultation before initiating the conflict, despite exposing allies and U.S. bases to retaliation, combined with Washington’s reluctance to defend partner countries. sources.headline: A Tale of Two Elon Musk Fights
sources.text:
Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report.
Here’s what’s on tap for the day: Elon Musk’s geopolitical fights in Ukraine and India, U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle resigns, and why Trump’s diesel deal won’t have much of an impact on fuel prices.
Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report.
Here’s what’s on tap for the day: Elon Musk’s geopolitical fights in Ukraine and India, U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle resigns, and why Trump’s diesel deal won’t have much of an impact on fuel prices.
Elon Musk keeps reminding us why so many people are uncomfortable with the degree of influence he holds over global geopolitics.
Nowhere is that truer than in Ukraine, which alleged this week that the billionaire’s company SpaceX had restricted some access to its Starlink satellite internet service—capping the speed at which Ukrainian weapons can remain connected to the internet in Kyiv’s ongoing war against Russia.
Musk claimed he wasn’t behind the restrictions, saying in a post on X that Ukraine’s military uses a military-grade version of Starlink called Starshield that is overseen by the U.S. government and that any decision to impose restrictions would have come from the Trump administration, not him. U.S. President Donald Trump has been pressuring Ukraine to stop strikes on Russia’s energy sector, as high gas prices cast a shadow over the upcoming U.S. midterm election. SpaceX and the Pentagon did not immediately respond to requests for comment from SitRep.
But the Ukraine brouhaha served as an acute reminder of how closely interlinked Musk and his businesses are with the U.S. government and how dependent multiple countries are on the whims of the world’s richest man. As Rishi has previously written, Starlink has been indispensable for the Ukrainian military and people, allowing the country to stay connected and in the fight since the early days of the war.
But Musk has also sometimes expressed sympathy for Russia’s perspective and echoed Kremlin talking points. He did so again on Wednesday, saying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky must “go” in response to Zelensky’s statement that he would not end the war until Russia was defeated.
“Even if you’re not 100 percent sure whether this was Elon Musk’s decision or whether it was the U.S. government’s decision, do you want to become dependent on a company whose head is inserting himself in your conflict?” Sharon Weinberger, the author of Valley of Death: How Big Tech Is Fueling the Future of War and the editor in chief of the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, told SitRep. “The problem is right now there just isn’t that much of an alternative,” she said. “Elon Musk, by virtue of having done things pretty well from a business standpoint, is in a dominant market position.”
As of Thursday, Starlink access for Ukraine’s military had reportedly been partially restored. That same day, Zelensky told the Financial Times that Ukraine was “done” respecting Trump’s demand to pause strikes on Russian energy targets.
That wasn’t Musk’s only geopolitical fight in recent days, however.
The India issue. While Ukraine fights to keep Starlink on, the world’s most populous country appears intent on keeping it out—much to Musk’s chagrin. The billionaire has spent years pushing for Starlink to gain a license to operate in India. He made some progress last year after he met Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in Washington, but the company is still waiting for final approvals.
But last Wednesday, Musk accused “certain oligarchs” in India of blocking Starlink from being approved “in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people.” Though he didn’t name names in that post, he made clear in later posts that he was referring to fellow billionaire Mukesh Ambani, a key Modi ally whose conglomerate owns India’s largest telecommunications company. Musk criticized Ambani’s “de facto monopoly in India” and sarcastically referred to him as the “real boss of India.”
Ironically, Starlink and Ambani’s company Reliance Jio already have a deal to bring Starlink to India, but neither company can proceed without a sign-off from Modi’s government. Ambani and his companies have not publicly responded to Musk’s accusations.
India shuts down the internet more frequently than almost any country in the world, and did so again this month to quell mass protests against Modi’s government—exactly the kind of internet curbs that Starlink has been used to circumvent in places like Iran. India’s communications ministry issued a statement after Musk’s initial accusations last week.
Though it didn’t mention the billionaire by name, it referred to a post “being circulated in social media regarding the fairness of India’s regulatory framework for satellite communication services and suggesting that it is being applied in a discriminatory manner.” The government refuted those claims, saying it had “put in place a fair and non-discriminatory authorisation framework” but said all providers are “required to demonstrate compliance with security conditions.”
For now, Musk will likely have to keep waiting.
Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned as U.S. ambassador to Greece this week following a string of negative headlines and allegations of improper conduct—including that she pressed a Republican donor to pay $100,000 to American Express to pay off her credit card balance prior to her Senate confirmation hearing.
“She was doing a good job, but we didn’t like what we were reading,” Trump said of Guilfoyle in comments to reporters on Tuesday.
What should be high on your radar, if it isn’t already.
Trump’s dud of a diesel deal. The surprise diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin that Trump announced last Friday has led to criticism on both sides of the Atlantic. Opponents worry the agreement will boost Putin’s war machine as Russia continues to pummel Ukraine. But Trump appears more concerned with being seen as taking action to lower energy costs ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. “Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority,” Trump said last week.
In a new piece this week, FP’s Keith Johnson explains why the controversial deal won’t significantly reduce fuel prices nor provide Moscow with major profits. Read it here.
Russia ramps up European sabotage. Moscow has consistently sought to punish Ukraine’s allies across Europe with acts of sabotage. These attacks initially targeted “symbolic objects,” but they have since entered a dangerous new phase that poses more of a threat to civilians, Margo Palloson, Estonia’s counterintelligence chief, told FP’s Sam Skove in a recent interview. Read it here.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky are seen standing outside of 10 Downing Street in London.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham greets Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky outside 10 Downing Street in London on Oct. 14.Henry Nicholls/WPA Pool/Getty Images
Monday, Oct. 19: The 2026 United Nations Biodiversity Conference is set to begin in Yerevan, Armenia.
Alberta is scheduled to hold a nonbinding referendum that will ask residents if they want to remain part of Canada.
Spain vs. Trump. FP editor in chief Ravi Agrawal spoke with Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares on the latest episode of FP Live about why the country’s left-wing government is willing to risk angering the world’s wealthiest country by standing up to Trump.
“We believe in international law. We believe that war shouldn’t be a tool used to achieve foreign-policy objectives,” the top Spanish diplomat said. FP Insiders can read that interview here. (Not an FP Insider yet? Subscribe here for your all-access pass to exclusive content, ad-free web browsing, and more perks.)
“My president—excuse me, my husband…”
—Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary, mistakenly referring to her husband as “my president” during her first White House press briefing.
To Understand France’s Unrest, Look Back to 1982 by Howard W. French
The Real Footprint of Trump’s Data Center Boom by Christina Lu
Russian Sabotage in Europe Is No Longer ‘Symbolic’ by Sam Skove

sources.headline: Surprise Starlink Cuts Blindside Kyiv
sources.text:
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the impact of Starlink limits on Ukraine’s defense, jail sentences for two leaders of India’s Cockroach movement, and Pope Leo XIV’s lung cancer diagnosis.
‘Badly Limited’
Ukraine on Wednesday said that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had abruptly limited the country’s access to its military-grade Starlink internet services without warning, undermining the country’s security. The Wall Street Journal reported that the new limits “restrict the speed at which some of Ukraine’s weapons can travel and still connect to the internet.” It is unclear why the restrictions were imposed now or when they might be lifted. However, the timing is likely to be damaging for Kyiv, which is preparing for a brutal winter defined by Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the impact of Starlink limits on Ukraine’s defense, jail sentences for two leaders of India’s Cockroach movement, and Pope Leo XIV’s lung cancer diagnosis.
‘Badly Limited’
Ukraine on Wednesday said that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had abruptly limited the country’s access to its military-grade Starlink internet services without warning, undermining the country’s security. The Wall Street Journal reported that the new limits “restrict the speed at which some of Ukraine’s weapons can travel and still connect to the internet.” It is unclear why the restrictions were imposed now or when they might be lifted. However, the timing is likely to be damaging for Kyiv, which is preparing for a brutal winter defined by Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Just two days after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, SpaceX activated Starlink in Kyiv and shipped its first terminals to the country. Despite SpaceX periodically restricting Ukraine’s access to its services, Kyiv has since come to rely on Starshield, a military-grade version of Starlink paid for by the U.S. Defense Department, to intercept Russian drone strikes and launch midrange attacks on Moscow.
According to senior Ukrainian officials and military personnel, signal failures early Wednesday disrupted several ongoing missions. “Logistics at the frontline and middle strikes are badly limited,” one senior official told the Financial Times. Ukrainian defense ministry advisor Serhii Beskrestnov stressed that long-range drone operations were also impacted.
Experts suspect that Wednesday’s limitations may have been ordered by the Pentagon, not SpaceX—a notion that Musk appeared to confirm later in the day. “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk wrote on X, using an acronym for the U.S. president. His statement came in response to an X post from former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who stated that some connectivity had been restored and had asked Musk to remove the speed limit entirely.
Ahead of the U.S. midterm elections next month, Trump has faced growing pressure to tackle rising fuel prices inflamed by the wars in Iran and Ukraine. He has repeatedly urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to halt all strikes on Russian oil refineries, and last Friday, he suspended U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel exports—a move condemned by U.S. lawmakers on both sides of the aisle. “This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies; it should be rescinded,” a dozen senators wrote to Trump on Tuesday.
Experts have previously suggested that the White House could cut off battlefield aid to Kyiv in an effort to force Zelensky to concede to some of Moscow’s demands and end the conflict. Whether the Trump administration would go so far as to make Starlink one of its bargaining chips, though, is unclear. The U.S. Defense Department, asked for comment on the restrictions before Musk’s X post, referred to Trump’s statement on Tuesday that the United States is continuing to share intelligence with Kyiv.
Meanwhile, Russia launched another devastating assault on critical Ukrainian infrastructure on Wednesday. Dozens of ballistic missiles targeted Kyiv’s energy facilities, plunging some 600,000 people across the capital into darkness. Repeated attacks on Ukraine’s power grid echo past Russian efforts to deprive Ukrainians of heat and water as the country prepares for its fifth winter at war.
Today’s Most Read
The Real Footprint of Trump’s Data Center Boom by Christina Lu
From Xinjiang to the Front Lines of Syria by Emily Feng
How JFK Helped Pave the Way for Trump’s Crackdown on Dissent by Julia Harte
What We’re Following
Behind bars. An Indian court ordered on Wednesday that two leaders of the so-called Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) be imprisoned for five days. They were arrested for trying to enter Jantar Mantar, a historic protest site that New Delhi has recently barred demonstrators from. The detentions risk further antagonizing anti-government protesters.
For months, the youth-led Cockroach movement has denounced lackluster job creation and poor education policy, including leaked medical exam results. However, protesters have recently shifted their attention to an election commission scandal, prompting some of New Delhi’s most heavy-handed crackdowns yet.
That has not stopped thousands of CJP supporters from taking to the streets in recent days, including Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, the two arrested CJP leaders who tried to “reclaim” Jantar Mantar from Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s control. “Why is Narendra Modi scared of Jantar Mantar?” Das wrote on X prior to his arrest. “Jantar Mantar belongs to THE PEOPLE OF INDIA.”
CJP leader Ajinkya Shinde, who was arrested with Das and Ranka but released on a personal bond, maintained that the movement would not be “frightened” by the sentencing. “We will put an end to this dictatorial ​government,” Shinde said. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke similarly denounced the court’s decision, accusing Modi of hiding behind “cowardly tactics.”
Cancer treatment. Pope Leo XIV underwent a successful surgery on Tuesday to remove part of his right lung following a cancer diagnosis. According to a Vatican spokesperson on Wednesday, the pope is expected to remain hospitalized for a week but has already begun respiratory physiotherapy, resumed his regular diet, and started walking around his room. “His recovery is proceeding as expected,” said the doctors in charge of Leo’s care at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital.
Leo was diagnosed with the early stages of lung adenocarcinoma, a kind of lung cancer that grows more slowly and usually forms on the outer layers of the organ. The 71-year-old revealed his diagnosis during Sunday’s noon prayer, breaking taboo by revealing his private medical issues in a public setting. It is unclear if Leo will still attend a two-week trip to South America next month, during which he was scheduled to visit 10 cities in Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru.
The health revelations have cast concerns on the longevity of Leo’s papacy. The Chicago-born pope was appointed at age 69, relatively young by papal standards. However, his cancer diagnosis has worried some Vatican analysts that the Church may need to begin considering a successor years before they were expecting to have to. Still, Leo’s doctors say that his prognosis looks optimistic.
Sinking ships. A Singapore-flagged vessel was transiting what Iran called an “unauthorized and dangerous route” through the Strait of Hormuz this week when it was struck by an unknown projectile and sank. According to the Maritime and Port ​Authority (MPA) of Singapore, a fire ignited on the GFS Pride, but all 21 crew members were safely evacuated.
Maritime officials on Wednesday also confirmed a separate attack on the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao, during which a projectile reportedly hit the bulk carrier on Sept. 23 and sank after an “unsuccessful rescue attempt,” said Vanguard, a British maritime risk management group.
“Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable, and a breach of international law,” Singapore’s MPA said on Wednesday, adding that it remains “deeply concerned” about continued targeted strikes on commercial shipping. Iran has repeatedly warned commercial vessels to steer clear of the Strait of Hormuz unless they have explicit approval from Tehran. U.S. forces have tried to guide ships through an alternative route that hugs Oman’s coast, but Iran has denounced such actions as circumventing its authority.
Odds and Ends
Hong Kong displayed a painting by Vincent van Gogh on Tuesday that has not been publicly exhibited in more than 60 years. Chestnut Trees in Blossom, completed in May 1890, is considered one of the most important works from the Dutch artist’s final days; van Gogh died two months later at age 37. Hundreds of people attended the unveiling ahead of its auction at New York’s Sotheby’s on Nov. 18. The painting is expected to bring in $180 million, exceeding van Gogh’s previous auction record of $117.2 million for Orchard with Cypresses.

sources.text: On the morning of October 14, Ukrainian soldiers began reporting restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite network that is essential for maintaining contact with drones moving at high speed. Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian president, said “this action can’t be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation,” referring to the conflict between Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump. On the morning of October 15, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said the system was working again. At the same time, no one in the United States has taken responsibility for the outage. sources.headline: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?
sources.text: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Starlink terminals, which connect to thousands of SpaceX satellites in obit, are often camouflaged on the battlefieldByTom McArthur and Tiffany WertheimerUpdated 15 October 2026 12:25 BSTStarlink satellites operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX provide high-speed internet - something modern war relies heavily on.For Ukraine, it is vital for communications on the battlefield and effective drone warfare.Using Starlink, Ukrainian drones can stay connected to operators over longer distances than conventional radio networks and are less vulnerable to jamming.But on Tuesday night, Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection. This disrupted some battlefield "missions", a top Ukrainian official said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks.The restriction at 100mph (160km/h) meant that any drone travelling faster than that lost connection and was effectively useless. "Starlink gives Ukraine the ability to see what's coming, to protect people," Kurt Volker, former US ambassador to Nato, told the BBC's Radio 4 Today programme. "If you cut that off, then more people are going to get killed - and that is a very cynical and callous decision to slow that down the way that has been done."Connectivity had been restored by Wednesday evening.The move has once again shown how Starlink can impact the conflict, which has been raging since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Operators use the Starlink network to stay connected to weapons like drones, so they can see targets in real timeWhat are Starlink and Starshield?Starlink is an internet network that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and battlefields. It currently relies on more than 10,000 active satellites, making Starlink the world's largest satellite constellation.It is owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, and is the company's biggest revenue driver.While Starlink is for civilian use, Starshield is its military-grade sister service, designed for the Pentagon. Starshield relies on the Starlink network, but has greater security like enhanced encryption so that sensitive information can be transmitted without interception.The US government has allowed Ukraine to use Starlink and Starshield in its defence against Russia. Musk cut Moscow's access to the service in February, giving Kyiv an advantage in the conflict.How does Starlink work on a battlefield?Put simply, Starlink uses its thousands of satellites to ping high-speed internet back to almost every corner of the globe, using terminals on the ground that users can easily buy and set up themselves. As Musk said, they have two instructions: "point at sky, plug in".This makes them ideal for use on the battlefield."It's a connection… that you can basically use pretty fast, you don't need any special equipment, you don't need to prepare, you just go to the field and usually it works," Neo, a soldier with one of Ukraine's drone reconnaissance units, told the Today programme."It simplifies our work because we can translate or stream our reconnaissance operations," he added.The network has become "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", George Barros from the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air forces.In Ukraine, both Starlink (the civilian service) and Starshield (the military service) are used, depending on what communications are needed.It is crucial for the effective use of weapons such as drones, which connect to the network so that operators can see their targets in real time, effectively minimising the time between "sensor-to shooter", Barros told the BBC.Because Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, when Ukraine sends long-range missiles deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.When it comes to Ukraine's self-defence, it relies on the Starlink network to protect its own skies against incoming Russian attacks, especially jet-powered Shahed drones, Barros added.Shaheds fly at speeds in excess of 198mph (319 km/h), meaning the Starlink restriction made Ukrainian efforts to chase them down all but impossible.For Neo, this means that any deliberate restrictions on the Starlink network are "a betrayal".With no ready replacement for the Starlink network, any speed restrictions or loss of connectivity have major implications for Ukraine defences, and the recent limits have shown how dependent Kyiv is on the network.Image source, Lev Radin/ Getty ImagesImage caption, Starlink terminals, like this one in Ukraine's Donetsk region, are quick and easy to set up, making them ideal for use on the battlefieldWhile Starlink can provide access nearly everywhere in the world, that does not mean it can be accessed everywhere, and countries must be licenced to use it.Russia is one place where it is not authorised, although Kyiv has in the past said that Moscow was still getting hold of the terminals and using them in occupied territory in Ukraine."If SpaceX obtains knowledge that Starlink terminal is being used by a sanctioned or unauthorized party, we investigate the claim and take actions to deactivate the terminal if confirmed," Starlink said in 2024.But with tens of thousands of terminals in Ukraine alone, it could be a near impossible task to determine which terminals are authorised and which ones are not.Why did Starlink restrict drone speeds?The answer remains unclear. During a visit to London on Wednesday, Zelensky had said he hoped it was just a mistake, however, in a later interview with the Financial Times, he said: "It was not a technical problem, it was the will."Musk said that Starshield is managed by the US government and suggested the Pentagon could be responsible."Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," he wrote on X, external. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS [the president of the United States]."He added: "Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."The BBC has contacted the White House and Pentagon for comment.Image source, EPAImage caption, A Ukrainian soldier attaches a Starlink transmitter to a 'Vampire' attack drone in the Donetsk region, eastern Ukraine, in JuneThe restrictions on Tuesday night came as Russia launched deadly attacks against Ukraine that left 600,000 without power and hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military. Residents said they received no warning of incoming drones before they hit."It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Zelensky's adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram on Wednesday morning.Relations between the US and Ukraine have worsened recently, especially since the US announced a deal with Russia to import its diesel into the American market.Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin, and in response Donald Trump said he thinks "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president".On Sunday, Trump announced a ceasefire on energy infrastructure, but three days later, Ukraine said it would resume the strikes, accusing Russia of ignoring it (the Kremlin said it had never agreed to a ceasefire), and the US of withdrawing crucial support.Zelensky has accused the US of threatening to withhold intelligence if Ukraine continues striking Russian oil facilities. Trump has denied this, but last week told reporters that Zelensky had "better damn well stop" the strikes.While in London, Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US.Trump's deal with Russia is his administration's latest effort to lower US fuel prices ahead of next month's midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war. That conflict, which started in February, has seen prices skyrocket, souring his standing with the American public.

sources.headline: Starlink: How Elon Musk's company influences geopolitics
sources.text:
Lack of internet access is a major problem in many regions of the world today.
Starlink was initially developed by the American tech billionaire Elon Musk to solve this problem. It was designed as a way of quickly getting the internet into regions all over the world where this was either impossible to do by conventional methods, or so expensive that it wasn't worth attempting.Starlink and SpaceX founder, controversial billionaire Elon MuskImage: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance
Since then, Starlink's field of application has widened significantly. It's used as a means of communication in disaster zones, but also by armies or protest movements, for example in regions where the existing internet has been destroyed by enemy fire or shut down by authoritarian governments.
But there is a downside: Ukraine's military, for example, is heavily dependent on Musk's satellite system. This has become especially apparent as the service faces external disruption.
How does Starlink work?
Starlink, which is operated by Musk's SpaceX company, is a satellite-based system consisting of 10,000 small satellites located around the world. They transfer data packages via laser links and do not require a constant, direct visual link to a ground station.
Unlike other internet satellites, which orbit at around 36,000 kilometers (22,000 miles) above the Earth, Starlink satellites are only about 550 kilometers up. This means they can transmit internet signals much faster than the others.
All users need is a small receiver terminal with an electronically controlled antenna, which automatically steers toward the satellites as they pass overhead. The terminals receive signals from these satellites and transmit them to a nearby router, which supplies the broadband internet connection.Starlink receivers smuggled into Iran enabled the opposition to organize despite the internet shutdownImage: Middle East Images/picture alliance
Where has Starlink already been deployed?
Ukraine: Since the start of the Russia's full-scale war in February 2022, Starlink has become a vital instrument of communication in the war zone. The Ukrainian armed forces use Starlink to coordinate units, operate drones and control unmanned ground systems. In the civilian sector, the system is used by hospitals, emergency services, energy suppliers and the railway network.
Ukraine offers a particularly vivid example of how heavily its military capabilities now depend on Starlink.
In mid-October, Ukrainian army units reported disruptions to data transmission, which are said to have severely affected the control of combat, interceptor- and reconnaissance drones. Elon Musk said that restrictions on the speed and use of Starlink are determined by the US military and ultimately the US president. At this stage, it remains unclear who ordered the restrictions.
Iran: In early January 2026, protests erupted all across the country against the regime in Tehran. The government's hardline response included a nationwide internet shutdown. Reportedly, thousands of Starlink terminals were smuggled into Iran and sold on the black market. This enabled the protest movement to go on coordinating demonstrations against the regime, using Starlink to circumvent state censorship of the internet.How reliable is Starlink as a wartime communications line?To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The country's authorities are cracking down on the satellite service and its users. Mohammad Amin Aghamiri, the secretary of the Supreme Council of Cyberspace, described Starlink as a hostile "tool of war" and said the regime had means at its disposal to disrupt satellite connections.
Starlink is officially banned in Iran. Anyone using the service faces a prison sentence of six months to two years. If users are also charged with endangering national security or espionage, the offence can even carry the death penalty.
Sudan: In the Sudanese civil war, Starlink is used primarily by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary group fighting against the internationally-recognized government. Hundreds of devices were smuggled into the country via the United Arab Emirates, and there is now a thriving black market for Starlink terminals in Sudan. The RSF use them to communicate and coordinate with their militias, while the Sudanese Armed Forces are trying to block both the import and use of the terminals.
Venezuela: Here too, Starlink has been used in the past to sidestep information blackouts and secure access to the internet. For a long time, the service was only available unofficially, by buying kits from local dealers. Following the US intervention in early January 2026, during which then-head of state, Nicolas Maduro, was taken prisoner, Musk offered the people of Venezuela a month's free broadband internet service via Starlink.
Gaza: Starlink has been used for humanitarian purposes in the devastated Gaza Strip since July 2024. Aid organizations and a field hospital use it to facilitate telemedical assistance and logistical coordination. Access for civilians remains limited because of Israeli security concerns.
Why has Starlink been criticized?
Starlink is often the only way to access the internet in conflict zones. This gives Musk and his operating company SpaceX tremendous influence. Previously, for example, Musk refused to activate Starlink in Ukraine to enable an attack in Crimea. US President Donald Trump has also threatened to switch off the satellites in Ukraine, as a way of forcing Kyiv to make concessions in peace negotiations.Starlink has provided vital communications for Ukrainian soldiers since the start of the 2022 Russian invasionImage: Alexander Polegenko/picture alliance
There has also been criticism from an ecological perspective. The Starlink satellites have a lifespan of less than five years. Every day, on average, one or two of them burn up in the Earth's atmosphere. This releases aluminum oxide, which could affect the ozone layer, contributing to global warming. In addition, all those thousands of satellites reflect the sunlight, making the night sky brighter, and this may also have repercussions for the world's animals.Any Starlink alternatives?
In an effort to break Starlink's monopoly, other companies, especially in Europe, are already working on alternatives. At present, the biggest private competitor to SpaceX is a company called Eutelsat. With a fleet of over 600 satellites, its OneWeb service is far smaller, focusing on business customers and maritime use.
But Eutelsat is also involved in the development of IRIS2 — an acronym for Infrastructure for Resilience, Interconnectivity and Security by Satellite, an ambitious EU project to establish a highly secure satellite network. The aim is to make Europe less dependent on Starlink, but IRIS2 won't be fully operational before 2032.
Elon Musk also has competition inside the US from another billionaire, Jeff Bezos, whose company Amazon is currently working on Amazon Leo, known until recently as Project Kuiper. This is establishing a network of more than 3,200 new low-Earth-orbit satellites. Amazon plans to roll out the service later this year in the US, Canada, France, Britain and Germany.Chinese competition for Starlink and SpaceX: The launch of a Chinese rocket carrying astronauts to a space station in April 2025Image: Andy Wong/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance
The sky is clearly getting crowded. China is also refining two satellite communications systems of its own. Guowang, a state project conceived primarily for national and military purposes, will consist of up to 13,000 satellites, while another project, Qianfan, with an estimated 12,000 satellites, is more commercially oriented and aims to provide services to newly industrialized and developing countries. The first mass starts for both of these projects are planned for this year.Will Russia have its own Starlink?
